How you show up is the work.

AI in practiceTeamworkQuality

Teaching AI to work like a project team

I kept hearing that AI would replace analysts, testers and delivery leads, so I wanted to find out for myself. I set AI up like a small project team (an analyst, a designer, a developer, a tester and a reviewer), each handing work to the next. I step in where judgement matters, and nothing ships without my sign off.

  1. Ready checkIs this ready to start?
  2. AnalystStories and what "done" looks like
  3. DesignerSpecs any screen change
  4. DeveloperBuilds it and checks its own work
  5. TesterTests against "done"
  6. ReviewerChecks everything, then I sign off

The problem

At first I used AI one chat at a time. Every new conversation meant explaining the whole project again, the quality depended on how tired I was that evening, and nothing stopped a weak answer slipping through.

What I did

I gave each role its own written playbook that says when it starts, what it needs and what it hands on. I added a "ready to start?" check at the front and a reviewer at the end who can send work back. A coordinator runs the chain and only comes to me when a decision is genuinely mine.

What worked

  • Agreeing the stories up front, so every role builds from the same picture
  • A reviewer with the power to send work back to whoever got it wrong
  • Writing my brand rules into the playbooks, so everything looks and sounds consistent

What didn't work

  • At first I switched roles by hand, and without one shared source of truth they slowly drifted apart
  • AI reads text from websites and documents, and some of that text can try to give it instructions. I had to design for that from day one

Lessons learned

  • The check matters more than the speed.
  • Agree what "done" means for each role before you automate it.
  • Treat anything AI reads as information, never as an instruction.
  • When something works, write it down so you never have to rebuild it.

The result

BeforeSwitching roles by hand, repeating myself, and no real quality check.
→
AfterOne brief in, one sign off out, with a proper review in between.
5roles that hand work to each other
1reviewer that can say no
5reusable playbooks

Connects to my why: AI did the legwork. Judgement, and knowing when to say no, stayed with me.

BuildingTestingLearning from failure

Building my own instructor app, and learning from what broke

Once Pass With Confidence had its first students, I needed one place to keep lesson notes, track progress and send each family a short recap. I built it myself, using the AI project team from the story above. This one is mostly about what went wrong, because that's where I learned the most.

  1. PlanI agree the stories
  2. BuildThe AI team works in short sprints
  3. TestIn a real browser, the way a user would
  4. ReleaseGoes live once approved

The problem

A learner's notes and progress need to live in one dependable place, and they can't disappear when the app is updated, restarted or something goes wrong. Families trust me with that information.

What I did

I built it in short sprints, with each AI role passing work to the next. I kept the technology deliberately simple so there was less to break, sent every progress update through one place, and made testing in a real browser part of every release.

What worked

  • Testing the app in a real browser, the way a user would, instead of only reading the code
  • A quick check that every file is valid before it goes anywhere
  • Checking a backup is complete before restoring anything from it

What didn't work

  • Old, unused copies of the page were hidden in the code, so some fixes landed in the wrong place
  • Logging out didn't work properly at first, and it took a few attempts to find a reliable fix
  • One way of releasing updates risked overwriting saved data, so I changed the approach before it could

Lessons learned

  • Test it like a user would. Reading the code is not enough.
  • Check a fix landed where you meant it to, not just that it exists.
  • Prove your data is safe before you change anything else.
  • Stop bad information at the door, before it can do damage.

The result

BeforeRebuilding progress notes and family recaps by hand after every lesson.
→
AfterOne app for students, lessons and progress, with checks that catch problems before anyone else does.
5AI roles building it
3hard lessons now written down as rules
1place for every learner's progress

Connects to my why: I learn by doing, then write the lesson down so it sticks.

BA craftVisual thinkingTeaching

My BA toolkit: one page visuals that help people see the work

In every project I've noticed the same thing: people agree much faster when they can see how the work flows on one page. So I started building my own library of one page visuals. I use them to keep learning, to prepare for interviews, and one day to teach others.

The library

Process maps

How work flows from start to finish, at a high level and one level down.

Role breakdowns

Who does what, where roles overlap, and where work tends to fall through the cracks.

Methods on a page

A BA technique and its templates, explained on a single page.

System comparisons

Platforms side by side, and what each one is genuinely good at.

Example of a level 1 map

  1. ElicitFind out what is needed
  2. AnalyseMake sense of it
  3. SpecifyWrite it down clearly
  4. ValidateCheck it with people
  5. SupportHelp it land

The problem

What I'd learned as a BA was scattered across old projects, notebooks and files. Whenever I needed it, for an interview or a new contract, I had to piece it together again.

What I did

I picked one simple format that opens on any device with nothing to install, gave every page the same header so it's easy to find, and set up one tidy folder structure. I deliberately kept it manual to start with, to see if the habit would stick.

What worked

  • Every visual opens anywhere, on a laptop or a phone
  • The same header on every page means I can find anything quickly
  • Keeping it completely separate from any employer's work, so I can share it freely

What didn't work

  • Filing everything by hand is slower. I chose that on purpose, until the habit proved it deserved a proper system
  • Because I keep the examples generic, I rebuild each one rather than reuse client work. It takes longer, but it keeps them clean

Lessons learned

  • One clear page beats ten detailed ones.
  • Pick the format first, and the content gets easier.
  • Build the habit before you automate it.

The result

BeforeKnowledge scattered across projects and files.
→
AfterA growing library of one page visuals I can hand to anyone, for learning, interviews and teaching.
5visuals so far, and growing
4types of visual
1page per idea

Connects to my why: Learn by doing, then turn it into something others can use.

Writing in public: why personal stories beat credentials

I post on LinkedIn to think out loud and to give something back. Early on I wrote about job titles and certifications, and they didn't really connect. When I started sharing real moments, like the rickshaw run or what I'd learned building with AI, they did. These are the themes I keep coming back to, and the rules I write by.

Theme

A rickshaw run as a change management masterclass

Daily huddles, constantly changing plans and a team of 108, and what that taught me about how people really take on change.

Theme

Claude is in my toolkit, not my replacement plan

How I use AI to stretch my thinking, not hand it over.

Theme

Going to the source on an AI incident

Reading past the headlines to the original report, and asking what it means for the AI tools I build myself.

The problem

Posts about job titles and credentials didn't connect with anyone. Posts built on a real moment from my life did.

What I did

I picked six themes I care about. Every post goes from rough idea to short brief to draft, and I've written down my own voice rules, so each draft starts out sounding like me, not like a brochure.

What worked

  • Opening with a real moment, then the lesson
  • Keeping the tone positive and focused on what changed
  • Ending with one simple question or next step for the reader

What didn't work

  • My early drafts were far too long for a phone screen, so now I cut every one back
  • Sometimes I reacted to the headline instead of the facts. Now I read the original source first
  • I haven't found a regular rhythm yet. For now I post when I have something real to say

Lessons learned

  • Only share what's true today, not what you plan to do.
  • The first two lines decide whether anyone reads on.
  • Read the source before you react.

The result

BeforeThe odd post, framed around job titles.
→
AfterPosts built on personal stories, in a voice that sounds like me.
6themes I keep coming back to
1set of voice rules I write by
2opening lines to earn the read

Giving backTeachingRunning a launch

Pass With Confidence: helping learner drivers find their confidence

As my children have grown up, I've had more time for my own goals. Teaching someone to drive felt like a meaningful way to give back, because it hands a person their independence. So I became a driving instructor, helping learners across Perth's northern suburbs become safe, confident and independent on the road. I ran the launch the way I'd run any project at work.

  1. CertifyInstructor certification
  2. EquipDual pedals fitted
  3. ProtectInsurance and lease sorted
  4. BookSimple online booking
  5. TeachLessons and mock tests

Watch

Meet your instructor in 13 seconds

This is the short video I send to learners before we meet. It puts a calm, friendly face to the name, shares what a real learner said about their lessons, and ends with an easy way to book.

The problem

Before the first lesson, a driving school has real hurdles to clear: certification, a car with dual controls, the right insurance, and a simple way for learners to book.

What I did

I earned my instructor certification, had dual pedals fitted, and worked through the insurance and lease requirements, comparing commercial cover options along the way. Then I set up online booking. I focus on the 6065 area and run mock tests near the Mirrabooka and Joondalup test centres.

What worked

  • Getting the compliance right first, and leaving marketing until after
  • Staying local, around the test centres my learners actually use
  • Planning a lesson and progress tracker with the same habits I use at work: clear stories and a shared idea of what "done" looks like

What didn't work

  • My booking system is only a link. It gives me no data and no confirmation email, so new bookings reach me as a text message
  • I started a simple website, then parked it in August to protect my focus

Lessons learned

  • Find out what a tool won't tell you before you rely on it.
  • Pausing a project on purpose is a decision, not a failure.
  • Sort out the boring compliance bits before you spend anything on marketing.

"His calm and collected approach creates a comfortable learning environment."Learner review, EzLicence, Sep 2026

Change managementLeadershipCharity

The rickshaw run: 2,100 km of change management, the hard way

In 2023 I joined 108 people, three to a rickshaw across 36 rickshaws, driving 2,100 km across northern India. We were raising money for SEWA UK, to help refurbish a dental unit in India that treats children with cleft defects. It was an adventure, a spiritual journey, an act of giving and a test of resilience, all rolled into one, and it taught me more about how people handle change than most programmes I've worked on.

Looking back through ADKAR, a common way of describing how people take on change

  1. AwarenessWhy we were there: a dental unit for children with cleft defects
  2. Desire108 people who chose to take this on
  3. KnowledgeMorning huddles shared the plan and reset the day
  4. AbilityChanging plans and handling problems on the road
  5. ReinforcementLooking out for each other kept everyone going

The problem

108 people in 36 rickshaws, crossing northern India together. The roads and the plan changed every day, and whatever happened, we had to sort it out ourselves.

What I did

I was team lead for 18 people across six rickshaws. I joined the morning huddles, helped solve problems as they came up, and kept everyone in the loop, from my own crew to the organisers. I tried to balance a clear plan with real care for how people were coping.

What worked

  • Morning huddles that shared the plan and reset the team every day
  • Talking to people in the way that worked for them, whether that was the organisers or a tired teammate
  • The whole group looking out for each other

What didn't work

  • Fixed plans rarely lasted the day
  • When something went wrong on the road, it had to be dealt with there and then, not scheduled for later

Lessons learned

  • Change is about people first, process second.
  • A clear plan and real care work together, not against each other.
  • A simple daily rhythm keeps a team moving through uncertainty.

The result

BeforeA route on a map.
→
After108 people in 36 rickshaws finished 2,100 km together and raised over GBP 750k for SEWA UK.
2,100 kmacross northern India
18people I led, across six rickshaws

TeachingRoot cause thinkingProgress tracking

How I teach driving: find the cause before adding practice

When a learner struggles, the instinct is to practise the same thing again. I've found it works better to work out why first, the same way I'd look for the root cause of a problem at work. This is the method I use, and the progress map I share with each learner's family.

The problem

A learner turns too early one time and too late the next. Practising the same turn over and over doesn't fix it, because the real cause isn't what it looks like.

What I did

I look at which of two things is happening. If the turn is sometimes early and sometimes late, the learner doesn't yet have a fixed point to judge it by. If it's always early, they have one, but it's in the wrong place. I show them where I'd look from my seat, then help them find their own point from theirs. They stay in full control of the car, and I take the pressure off by choosing quiet streets and giving the directions.

What worked

  • A simple role swap: I drive, and the learner calls out the moment to start the turn. That skill carried straight over to judging gaps for right turns
  • Showing rather than telling, with small reference cards in the car instead of homework
  • Teaching learners to slow down by easing off the accelerator, not reaching straight for the brake

What didn't work

  • Mixing left and right turns in one lesson muddied things, so now I keep them separate
  • My first progress recaps listed skills we hadn't started yet. That set the wrong expectations, so I took them out

Lessons learned

  • Work out the cause before you add more practice.
  • Let learners find their own reference points. They stick better than mine.
  • Show progress honestly, only for skills you've actually started.

The result

BeforeA general impression at the end of each lesson.
→
AfterA clear record of every lesson, a progress map, and an honest summary for the learner's family.
1recap template for every learner
1progress map, previous lesson against latest
0homework, everything is shown in the car

Connects to my why: giving back, and showing people what else is possible for them.

Wheel of life: see the whole picture, then pick one thing

The wheel of life is a classic coaching exercise: you score eight areas of your life and see where things are out of balance. I've made it interactive, so you can try it right here. Move the sliders and the wheel redraws.

Try it

Score each area from 1 to 10. The values below are examples. Nothing you enter is saved or sent anywhere.

5
5
5
5
5
5
5
5

The problem

When life feels busy but stuck, it's hard to know where to start. Seeing everything in one picture makes the conversation more honest, whether it's with a coach, a partner or yourself.

What I did

I built a wheel with eight areas that redraws as you score. It names your strongest and lowest areas, then asks for just one small action, not a full plan. My partner and I use it regularly, so we stay aligned on what matters to each of us.

What worked

  • Eight areas are enough to spot a pattern, and few enough to finish
  • Asking for one small action, rather than a long plan, makes it far more likely to happen

Design choices

  • There's no overall score, because a single number hides the story
  • Nothing you enter is saved or sent anywhere, so you can be honest

Lessons learned

  • Balance is a picture before it's a plan.
  • Start with your lowest area, but change only one thing.
  • A score starts a conversation; it isn't a verdict.

The result

BeforeA vague feeling of being busy and stuck.
→
AfterA clear picture of where you are, and one small action for this month.
8life areas on the wheel
1small action to pick
0data stored or sent

Connects to my why: curiosity and learning by doing. It's the same habit I use at work: see the whole picture before you fix one part.

HealthConsistencyBeing coached

My fitness journey: a marathon, not a race

In 2023 I started a coached fitness programme with RNT Fitness. I've learned a lot, slipped up a lot and bounced back each time, moving forward one step at a time. Funnily enough, the habits that help most are the same ones I rely on at work.

  1. LogMeals and training, all in one place
  2. AverageJudge the week, not the day
  3. Check inShare it with my coach
  4. AdjustMy coach tweaks the plan
  5. RepeatOne step at a time

The problem

I started and stopped more than once. Looking for quick fixes, stepping on the scale every day and losing sight of why I'd started did more damage than any lack of effort.

What I did

I worked with a coach on a structured plan: four meals a day, everything logged in one app, and progress judged on the average over seven days rather than any single day. In the gym I followed one simple rule for when to lift heavier. I took a planned break to hold steady, then restarted with something to aim for: the 350 km charity road ride with friends.

What worked

  • Looking at the weekly average instead of the daily number
  • One log and one coach, so anything that goes off plan gets talked about, not hidden
  • A simple gym rule: once I hit 12 reps, I add weight
  • Walking and training as fixed points, even in busy weeks

What didn't work

  • I stalled and eased off more than once, and a planned break went on longer than it should have
  • When the scale didn't move, I wanted to change the plan myself instead of talking to my coach
  • As a vegetarian, hidden surprises like animal products in restaurant sauces sometimes knocked me off course

Lessons learned

  • Consistency beats intensity.
  • Trust the trend, not the day.
  • Give the effort a reason that matters, like an event with a date.
  • Raise problems early with the person who owns the plan.
  • Every restart is a lesson, not a defeat.

The result

BeforeStarting over again and again, chasing the number on the scale.
→
AfterA weekly rhythm I can repeat, and a journey that's still moving forward, one step at a time.
2023the year I started
4meals a day, all in one log
7day average, the only trend I trust

About me

Why I do it, and how I show up

I'm curious by nature and I learn by doing. Whatever I learn at work ends up at home, and the other way round. It all goes back to something my dad told us growing up.

Anything is possible. My dad made sure we heard it, and I've been testing it ever since.

  1. CuriousI keep asking what else is possible
  2. Learn by doingI try it for real, not just read about it
  3. ApplyI use it at work and at home
  4. ConnectWork and life feed each other

Four habits behind the work

I don't stay in one lane. My best results have come from seeing how the pieces fit together before anyone started building.

1

See the whole chain

I follow a problem from the first request to the final outcome. The gaps between teams and tools are where projects quietly fail.

2

Build in the check first

Speed is easy to come by these days, especially with AI. Quality isn't. So I decide how we'll check the work before we start producing it.

3

Learn alongside the doers

Standing next to people who are already doing the thing teaches me faster than any book. I look for rooms that stretch me.

4

Try small, write it down

I try things in small steps, keep the lesson, and write down what works so I never have to solve the same problem twice.

What I got wrong

The cheapest way to learn is from someone else's mistakes. Here are a few of mine, and what I do differently now.

Mistake

I relied on a tool I couldn't see inside

My booking system is just a link. It gives me no data and no confirmation email, so I only hear about new bookings by text.

Now: I list what a tool can't do before I start relying on it.

Mistake

I let my AI roles drift apart

I switched between AI roles by hand, with nothing tying them together, and bit by bit each one rewrote the brief its own way.

Now: every role works from one agreed set of stories, with a review at the end.

Mistake

I wrote like a brochure

My early posts were polished, and completely forgettable.

FAQ

Questions people ask

What do you actually do?

I'm a senior business analyst, and I work end to end: from understanding the problem, through requirements and delivery, to making sure the change actually lands. Most of my job is connecting people, process and systems. I use AI where it genuinely helps, so more of my time goes on judgement and on the people involved.

Will AI replace business analysts?

I don't think so. AI can write a requirement, but it can't read a room, build trust with a nervous stakeholder or hold a team together when the plan changes. Organisations that cut their BAs, PMOs and delivery leads, expecting AI to fill the gap, are likely to learn that the hard way. The value was never just in the documents. It's in how you show up.

How do you use AI in your work?

Where it helps, not everywhere. I saw plenty of posts about how AI would change the way we work, and very little evidence from people actually trying it, so I decided to try it for real. In my own projects AI works like a small team: each role has a written playbook and hands work to the next, and there's a review before anything is finished. I stay in charge of the direction and the final sign off. Plenty of my work I still do without it.

How do you manage the risks of AI?

I treat anything AI reads, from a website or a document, as information, never as an instruction to follow. A person always signs off, there's a proper review before anything is final, and I read up on real incidents so I can design for them early.

Why take on projects outside work?

Because that's where I learn fastest. Teaching learner drivers and building a small business end to end means I practise discovery, compliance, tools and delivery with real people and real consequences. Everything I learn there comes back to my day job, and it keeps me close to the people a change is actually for.
